steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our discrete mathematics paper on reducing asynchronous Boolean networks by eliminating variables, extending the standard elimination to negatively autoregulated components. Motivate model reduction, explain the existing approach and our extension with its properties, discuss attractor preservation for intermediate (mediator) nodes, and give the paper outline.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Growing regulatory network models and the analysis problem
- Reduction strategies: trap spaces vs. fast updates / variable elimination
- Our extension to negatively autoregulated variables and its properties
- Attractor preservation and simple mediator nodes
- Paper outline

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Growing models
  - powerful molecular genetics technologies -> large data -> larger models of regulatory networks
  - problems for analysis; esp. quantitative models (differential or stochastic, cite), but qualitative too
  - logical models widely used (cite)
- Reduction strategies
  - combinatorial explosion with number of components -> rigorous analysis unattainable
  - reduce network size; two main strategies
  - 1: trap spaces = invariant subspaces of state space (cite)
  - 2 (our focus): some updates faster than others; Boolean and multi-valued case (cite)
  - Boolean: substitute variable with expression of its update rule; only if not autoregulated
  - asynchronous state transition graph: no autoregulation -> each pair of neighbour states differing in eliminated variable has exactly one source of transition changing it; other = target = "representative" state; transitions from representatives preserved
- Our extension
  - natural extension to negatively autoregulated variables
  - pair of neighbour states may be connected both directions -> no representative needed; same strongly connected component -> transitions from either state preserved
  - effect on interaction graph similar to original, differences re introduction of loops
  - fixed point preservation refined: two-state attractors can collapse to one
  - total number of attractors cannot decrease (as original)
  - alternative proof of result due to Richard (cite): bound on number of attractors via cardinality of positive feedback vertex sets of interaction graphs
- Attractor preservation
  - reduced networks of the method (cite) easy to compute -> very large networks
  - fixed points always preserved (non-autoregulated) but dynamics can change significantly
  - effort on structural conditions guaranteeing all attractors preserved
  - merging vertices with in- and outdegree one (cite): simple mediator nodes (cite), also linear variables (cite)
  - we show cases where attractors not preserved, despite claim (cite)
  - doesn't impact usefulness of method (cite): counterexamples quite artificial
- Outline
  - Section 2: notation, properties of reduction method (cite)
  - generalisation to negative autoregulation, simple proof of attractor bound (Section 3)
  - Section 4: cyclic attractors under elimination of intermediate components, with/without negative autoregulation

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
With more and more powerful technologies in molecular genetics, it is possible to get large amounts of data, and this leads to larger and larger models of complex regulatory networks. This creates problems and limitations for the analysis of these models. This is especially true for quantitative models (e.g., differential or stochastic models), but qualitative models are also more and more affected. Among qualitative models, logical models are widely used.

Even though these models are simple, the combinatorial explosion as the number of components increases makes the rigorous analysis of many models unattainable. One way to deal with this problem is to reduce the size of the original network. There are two main strategies that are used. The first one is based on trap spaces, i.e. invariant subspaces of the state space. The second approach, which is the one we focus on here, is based on the assumption that some of the updates, i.e. changes in the components, happen faster than others. This idea was developed for the Boolean case and also for the more general multi-valued case. In the Boolean formalism, the method allows a variable to be substituted with the expression that defines its update rule. This is only possible if the variable is not autoregulated. In terms of asynchronous state transition graphs, when there is no autoregulation it is guaranteed that, for each pair of neighbour states that differ in the variable being eliminated, exactly one of the two states is the source of a transition that changes the value of the variable being eliminated. So the other state is the target of this transition, and it can be chosen as the "representative" state; the elimination preserves all transitions from representative states.

In this setting, we see that there is a natural way to extend the elimination to variables that are negatively autoregulated. When there is a possible negative autoregulation, a pair of neighbour states that differ in the variable being eliminated can be connected by transitions in both directions. In that case a representative does not have to be chosen, and since the two states are in the same strongly connected component, the transitions from either of the two states can be preserved in the reduction. The elimination method we introduce in this work implements this idea. We show that this extended method affects the interaction graph in a similar way as the original reduction method, with some differences that can concern the introduction of loops. The preservation of fixed points has to be refined to account for attractors made of two states that can collapse to one, but we prove that the total number of attractors cannot decrease with the reduction, just like for the original method. With these properties, we give an alternative proof for a result due to Richard, which gives a bound on the number of attractors of asynchronous Boolean networks in terms of the cardinality of positive feedback vertex sets of the interaction graphs.

- Attractor preservation
  - reduced networks of the existing method (cite) easy to compute -> very large networks
  - fixed points always preserved (non-autoregulated) but dynamics can change significantly
  - conditions on structure guaranteeing all attractors preserved
  - merging vertices with in- and outdegree one (cite): simple mediator nodes (cite), also linear variables (cite)
  - counterexamples where attractors not preserved, despite claim (cite); method still useful (cite), counterexamples artificial
- Outline
  - Section 2: notation, properties of reduction method (cite)
  - Section 3: generalisation to negative autoregulation, simple proof of attractor bound
  - Section 4: cyclic attractors under elimination of intermediate components

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
With more and more powerful technologies in molecular genetics, it is possible to get large amounts of data, and this leads to larger and larger models of complex regulatory networks. This creates problems and limitations for the analysis of these models. This is especially true for quantitative models (e.g., differential or stochastic models), but qualitative models are also more and more affected. Among qualitative models, logical models are widely used.

Even though these models are simple, the combinatorial explosion as the number of components increases makes the rigorous analysis of many models unattainable. One way to deal with this problem is to reduce the size of the original network. There are two main strategies that are used. The first one is based on trap spaces, i.e. invariant subspaces of the state space. The second approach, which is the one we focus on here, is based on the assumption that some of the updates, i.e. changes in the components, happen faster than others. This idea was developed for the Boolean case and also for the more general multi-valued case. In the Boolean formalism, the method allows a variable to be substituted with the expression that defines its update rule. This is only possible if the variable is not autoregulated. In terms of asynchronous state transition graphs, when there is no autoregulation it is guaranteed that, for each pair of neighbour states that differ in the variable being eliminated, exactly one of the two states is the source of a transition that changes the value of the variable being eliminated. So the other state is the target of this transition, and it can be chosen as the "representative" state; the elimination preserves all transitions from representative states.

In this setting, we see that there is a natural way to extend the elimination to variables that are negatively autoregulated. When there is a possible negative autoregulation, a pair of neighbour states that differ in the variable being eliminated can be connected by transitions in both directions. In that case a representative does not have to be chosen, and since the two states are in the same strongly connected component, the transitions from either of the two states can be preserved in the reduction. The elimination method we introduce in this work implements this idea. We show that this extended method affects the interaction graph in a similar way as the original reduction method, with some differences that can concern the introduction of loops. The preservation of fixed points has to be refined to account for attractors made of two states that can collapse to one, but we prove that the total number of attractors cannot decrease with the reduction, just like for the original method. With these properties, we give an alternative proof for a result due to Richard, which gives a bound on the number of attractors of asynchronous Boolean networks in terms of the cardinality of positive feedback vertex sets of the interaction graphs.

The reduced networks of the existing method can be computed quite easily, so the approach can be applied to very large networks. Fixed points are always preserved when variables that are not autoregulating are eliminated, but in some cases this reduction approach can change the dynamics of the networks a lot. So some effort has gone into finding conditions on the structure of the network that guarantee that a reduction preserves not only fixed points but all attractors. Some authors suggested merging vertices that have in- and outdegree one, which are called simple mediator nodes (or linear variables). Here we look at these assumptions in detail and show that unfortunately there are still some cases where attractors are not preserved, despite what was claimed. This result does not affect the usefulness of the method suggested by these authors, because such counterexamples can be quite artificial.

In Section 2 we set up the notation we need and briefly summarise some properties of the existing reduction method. Then we introduce a generalisation of this reduction method that can be applied to variables with negative autoregulation, and we use it to get a simple proof for a bound on the number of attractors of Boolean networks (Section 3). In Section 4 we discuss whether cyclic attractors are preserved when intermediate components are eliminated, with or without negative autoregulation.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
With increasingly powerful technologies in molecular genetics it is possible to obtain large amounts of data, which lead to increasingly larger models of complex regulatory networks. This poses problems and limitations for the analysis of such models. While this applies especially to quantitative models (e.g., differential or stochastic models [1,2,3]), qualitative models are also increasingly affected; among the latter, logical models are widely used [4,5,6,7].

Despite their simplicity, the combinatorial explosion that comes with an increasing number of components makes the rigorous analysis of many models unattainable. One approach to this problem consists in reducing the size of the original network, and there are mainly two strategies in use. The first relies on trap spaces, i.e. invariant subspaces of the state space [8]. The second, on which we focus here, relies on the assumption that some of the updates, i.e. changes in the components, happen faster than others. This idea has been developed for the Boolean as well as the more general multi-valued case [9,10,11]. In the Boolean formalism, the method allows a variable to be substituted with the expression defining its update rule, which is only possible if the variable is not autoregulated. In terms of asynchronous state transition graphs, the absence of autoregulation guarantees that, for each pair of neighbour states that differ in the variable being eliminated, exactly one of the two states is the source of a transition that changes the value of that variable. The other state is therefore the target of this transition and can be selected as the "representative" state; all transitions from representative states are preserved by the elimination. In this setting, we observe that there is a natural way of extending the elimination to negatively autoregulated variables. In presence of a possible negative autoregulation, a pair of neighbour states that differ in the variable being eliminated can be connected by transitions in both directions. It is then not necessary to choose a representative, and since the two states belong to the same strongly connected component, transitions from either state can be preserved in the reduction. The elimination method introduced in this work implements this idea. We show that the extended method affects the interaction graph in a similar way to the original reduction method, with some differences that can concern the introduction of loops. While the preservation of fixed points needs to be refined to account for attractors consisting of two states that can collapse to one, we prove that, as for the original method, the total number of attractors cannot decrease with the reduction. Using these properties, we give an alternative proof of a result due to Richard [12] that bounds the number of attractors of asynchronous Boolean networks in terms of the cardinality of positive feedback vertex sets of the interaction graphs.

The reduced networks of the method introduced in [9,10,11] can be computed quite easily, which makes the approach applicable to very large networks. While fixed points are always preserved by the elimination of variables that are not autoregulating, in some cases the reduction can change the dynamics of the networks significantly. Some effort has therefore been invested in finding conditions on the network structure that guarantee that a reduction preserves not only fixed points but all attractors. In [13,14], the authors suggested merging vertices with in- and outdegree one, so-called simple mediator nodes [14] (also called linear variables in [15]). Here we take a detailed look at these assumptions and show that, unfortunately, there are still certain cases where attractors are not preserved, despite the claim in [14]. This result does not impact the usefulness of the method suggested in [13,14], since such counterexamples can be quite artificial.

In Section 2 we set the required notation and briefly summarise some properties of the reduction method described in [9,10,11]. We then introduce a generalisation of this method that applies to variables with negative autoregulation and use it to derive a simple proof of a bound on the number of attractors of Boolean networks (Section 3). In Section 4 we discuss the preservation of cyclic attractors under the elimination of intermediate components, with or without negative autoregulation.
